readerTitle: The car dealer who saw $332,000 in every customer
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Sewell 자동차 딜러, Carl Sewell의 책) + 가상 적용 (가사 청소 서비스, 일정 관리 앱)
insight: 고객 한 명은 한 번의 거래가 아니라 여러 해에 걸친 구매의 흐름이다. 그래서 '이번 거래에서 얼마 남나'가 아니라 '얼마나 오래 머무나'를 먼저 묻는다.
misconception: 첫 거래에서 손해 보는 고객 확보 비용은 무조건 나쁜 지출이다.

sources.text: Sewell, C. & Brown, P. B. (1990). Customers for Life. Doubleday.
평균 고객 수명 ≈ 1 ÷ 월 이탈률: 구독·반복 매출 분석의 표준 근사식
청소 서비스와 일정 관리 앱 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Carl Sewell이 『Customers for Life』(1990)에서 고객 한 명의 평생 가치를 약 $332,000로 추정했다는 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요. 수치가 판본마다 다르면 카드 문구를 'more than $300,000'로 바꿉니다.
Sewell이 댈러스의 캐딜락 딜러였다는 점, 이 추정에 차량 구매와 정비·서비스 비용이 포함됐다는 점을 확인하세요.
앱 계산: 월 이탈률 8% → 평균 수명 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5개월, × $25 = $312.50. 이탈률 4% → 25개월, × $25 = $625. 차이 $312.50 > 온보딩 비용 $200. 할인율(미래 돈의 가치)은 단순화를 위해 무시했습니다.

cards.title: The car dealer who saw $332,000 in every customer
body: In his 1990 book *Customers for Life*, Dallas car dealer Carl Sewell did an odd sum. He added up every car and every service visit a loyal customer might buy from him over a lifetime.
His estimate was about $332,000. The person at the counter wasn't one sale. They were decades of sales, if they stayed.

image.label: One customer followed by a long trail of future purchases
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 자동차 매장 카운터 앞의 고객 한 명 뒤로 작은 자동차, 정비 공구, 영수증들이 시간순으로 길게 줄지어 이어짐. 실제 자동차 브랜드 로고나 엠블럼은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Is $150 too much for one new customer?
body: You run a house cleaning service. Clients pay $120 a visit, every two weeks. After wages and supplies, each visit leaves you $40.
A local lead site offers you new clients for $150 each. The first visit only earns $40. Do you sign up?

options.text: No. You lose $110 on every new client
options.feedback: True for the first visit only. You protect this month's cash, but you may turn away clients who would earn you far more over time.

options.text: First check how long your clients usually stay
options.feedback: The deal is good or bad depending on that one number. It takes a little digging, but it turns a guess into a decision.

options.text: Yes. Regular cleaning clients always come back
options.feedback: Right that repeat visits matter. But clients from a lead site may stay for a shorter time than your referrals, so check before you assume.

cards.title: Follow one cleaning client.
body: Your records show clients stay about 18 months on average. The $150 is paid back after four visits, in about two months. Everything after that is yours.

breakdown.label: Visits

cards.title: Customer lifetime
body: **Customer lifetime** is how long a customer keeps buying from you. Multiply it by what each period leaves after costs, and you get what a customer is worth.

A quick estimate: if 5% of customers leave each month, the average one stays about 20 months (1 ÷ 0.05). Sewell's insight was to judge every decision against that whole stream, not the sale in front of him.

image.label: A single sale versus a long row of repeat sales
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에는 동전 하나와 "One visit: $40", 오른쪽에는 시간축 위에 동전이 길게 쌓여 "Lifetime: $1,560". 오른쪽이 훨씬 크게 보이도록.

cards.title: Lifetime tells you what a customer is worth fighting for.
body: Once you see the lifetime, small choices look different. A free fix for an angry customer costs a little today and protects years of future business.

Sewell argued exactly this: treat the customer so they come back for the next car, and the next service. The same sum tells you how much you can spend to win a customer, and how much to spend keeping one.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams compare customer lifetime value with the cost to win a customer. Because churn is tracked monthly, lifetime can be estimated early, then checked as real data comes in.

cards.title: An average lifetime can fool you.
body: Averages hide spread. Some clients leave after one visit, others stay five years. Clients from a cheap lead source may behave very differently from referrals.

A young business has little history, so its lifetime figure is mostly a guess. Use margin, not price, in the sum. And money that arrives in year three is worth less, and less certain, than money today.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling app.
body: Your app costs $30 a month and leaves $25 after costs. About 8% of users cancel each month, so they stay about 12.5 months.
A setup call for each new user costs $200. Tests suggest it cuts monthly churn to 4%. Worth it?

options.text: No. $200 is almost seven months of revenue
options.feedback: It is a big upfront cost. But it ignores that users would now stay about 25 months instead of 12.5.

options.text: Yes. Lifetime doubles, adding about $312 per user
options.feedback: Value rises from $312 to $625, well above the $200 cost. Keep checking that the churn drop holds beyond the test.

options.text: Spend the $200 on ads for more new users instead
options.feedback: More users helps, but each one still leaves after about a year. Longer lifetimes make every future ad dollar work harder too.

cards.title: A customer is a stream, not a sale.
body: How long customers stay decides what each one is worth, and what you can afford to spend winning and keeping them.
**Try it today:** estimate how long your average customer stays. Multiply by what each month or visit leaves after costs. Compare it with what you pay to win one.
